passage: Monday. Samir won the college data-modelling contest by a mile. The same evening, his sister Farida found the scholarship form, unsigned, under a pile of chip packets. The deadline had passed at noon. Thursday. Farida came home in tears after a bad viva. Samir listed five ways to prepare better next time. She snapped, "I didn't ask you to fix me!" and slammed her door. He sat in the corridor, puzzled and hot-faced. The next Sunday. Samir wrote two lists on the whiteboard: things I'm great at, and things I'm still learning. Organising and "knowing when someone just wants listening" went on the second. He didn't erase them. He set phone reminders for every form. Then he knocked on Farida's door. "Do you want advice, or just company?" "Company," she said, and moved over.

qa.q: What did Samir win on Monday?
qa.a: The college data-modelling contest, by a mile.

qa.q: How did Samir feel after Farida slammed her door, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt confused and embarrassed; he sat in the corridor puzzled and hot-faced.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Samir?
qa.a: He listed his strengths and gaps without erasing them, set reminders for forms, and asked Farida whether she wanted advice or company.

qa.q: How might Farida see Samir's question 'advice, or just company?'
qa.a: She likely feels understood, since he is now asking what she needs instead of trying to fix her.

grounding: It shows a young adult brilliant at analysis who struggles with organisation and emotional skills, and who looks at strengths and gaps without shame to work on each.

passage: "Jeevan, sit down. You missed one deadline, you didn't set the lab on fire. When I was your age, I could build a model from any messy data in a night. Our professor called me the sharpest in the batch. And I missed three project meetings in one month because I never wrote anything down. Once I made a junior cry by telling her, flat, that her code was useless. I didn't even notice until someone told me. I felt ashamed, and I wanted to hide in the numbers. My supervisor didn't let me. She said, 'Nilesh, you have a brilliant head and a messy diary. Both are true. Fix the diary.' So I got a paper planner, and I started asking juniors, 'Can I give feedback now?' Thirty years later, I still use the planner."

qa.q: What did Nilesh's supervisor say to fix?
qa.a: The diary.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel on learning about making a junior cry?
qa.a: Nilesh felt ashamed and wanted to hide in the numbers.

qa.q: What steps did Nilesh take after the supervisor's words?
qa.a: Nilesh got a paper planner and began asking before giving feedback, working on each gap without shame.

qa.q: How might the junior have felt when Nilesh said, flat, that her code was useless?
qa.a: The junior probably felt hurt and small, enough to cry, since the words judged the whole code and offered no help.

grounding: An elder recalls being brilliant at analysis but weak at organisation and emotional skills, and learning to see strengths and gaps without shame.

passage: In the small town of Malerkotla, Dilnaz, twenty, ran the numbers for her family's dairy cooperative. She could spot a cheating supplier from one column of figures. But she forgot meeting dates, lost the receipt book twice, and when her cousin Farhan came to her upset about failing his driving test, she said, "Just practise the reversing. It's simple." He walked out. That night she felt ashamed, twice over. Her aunt said, "You are sharp as a knife, Dilnaz, and sometimes you cut." Instead of sulking, Dilnaz made a wall calendar with coloured pins. Then she went to Farhan's room. "I was blunt. I'm sorry. Tell me how it felt?" He looked surprised, then started talking.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz make to handle her forgetfulness?
qa.a: She made a wall calendar with coloured pins.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel that night, and why?
qa.a: She felt ashamed twice over, for being disorganised and for hurting Farhan with a blunt reply.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz do that shows working on gaps without shame?
qa.a: She accepted her aunt's point, made a practical calendar and apologised to Farhan, asking how he felt.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt when Dilnaz came to apologise?
qa.a: He was surprised and probably relieved and cared for, which is why he started talking.

grounding: Shows a young adult brilliant at analysis who struggles with organisation and emotional skills, and works on both without shame.

passage: In a student flat in Copenhagen, Lars, twenty-one, solved problem sets his physics professor called "graduate level." He also missed the deadline to register for his own exams, because the email sat unread among two hundred others. The same week his flatmate Yosef's grandmother died. Lars listened for ten seconds and started explaining how to book the cheapest flight. Yosef said quietly, "I didn't need a plan, I needed you to just sit here." Lars felt his face burn. He went to the university's study support office the next day and set up a weekly planning session. And that evening he knocked on Yosef's door, sat on the floor and said nothing for a long time. Yosef passed him a cup of tea.

qa.q: Why did Lars miss the exam registration deadline?
qa.a: The email sat unread among two hundred others.

qa.q: How did Lars feel when Yosef said he just needed company?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and ashamed, his face burning as he realised he had missed what Yosef needed.

qa.q: How did Lars work on his gaps without giving up on himself?
qa.a: He went to study support for weekly planning, and he returned to Yosef to simply sit with him.

qa.q: What was it like for Yosef when Lars came and sat quietly?
qa.a: Yosef likely felt comforted and cared for, which he showed by passing Lars a cup of tea.

grounding: Shows a young adult brilliant at analysis who struggles with organisation and emotional skills at once, facing both without shame and working on each.

passage: At the college hackathon, Jatin, nineteen, cracked the routing algorithm at 3 a.m. that had stumped every team. At 5 a.m. he discovered he'd saved it nowhere. His teammate Aditi found him staring at the screen. "It's gone. I'm useless," he said. Aditi, the team lead, had been tired and snappy herself all night, and he hadn't noticed. She sat down. "You're brilliant at the hard part, and you're terrible at saving files. Both are true. Rewrite it; I'll set up auto-save." He rewrote it in forty minutes. Later, he said, "You were upset last night, weren't you? I missed that." Aditi smiled. "You're learning." They came second, and Jatin kept a sticky note on his laptop: SAVE. ASK.

qa.q: What did Jatin write on his sticky note?
qa.a: He wrote SAVE. ASK.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel when he found his work was not saved?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and hopeless, calling himself useless.

qa.q: How did Aditi help Jatin see his strengths and gaps without shame?
qa.a: She named both honestly, that he is brilliant at algorithms and bad at saving files, then helped fix the practical gap.

qa.q: How might Aditi feel when Jatin asks about her mood?
qa.a: She may feel noticed and pleased, seeing that he is working on reading other people's feelings.

grounding: Shows a young adult with brilliant analysis but weak organisation and emotional awareness, helped to see both without shame and work on each.

passage:
Dear Professor Sharmila,
I wanted to explain the late submission and what happened in the group meeting.
You've said my analysis of the survey data was the best in the cohort. I believe the numbers part is strong. But I lost the final draft twice because my files are everywhere, and I missed two deadlines this term.
Then, when Kunal disagreed with my model, I said his idea was "obviously wrong" in front of everyone. I didn't notice he was upset until he left. I felt so ashamed that I skipped the next meeting.
I've been thinking. Maybe I'm not "brilliant but careless". Maybe I'm strong at analysis and still learning organisation and how people hear me. I've started a weekly file check and I apologised to Kunal.
Could I meet you to plan the rest of the project?
Irawati

qa.q: How many deadlines did Irawati miss this term?
qa.a: Two deadlines.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel after noticing Kunal was upset?
qa.a: Irawati felt deeply ashamed, so much that the next meeting was skipped.

qa.q: What change in thinking helps Irawati work on the gaps?
qa.a: Seeing strengths and gaps without shame, so Irawati can keep the analysis skills while practising organisation and how words land.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt in the meeting?
qa.a: He was likely hurt and embarrassed to have his idea called obviously wrong in front of everyone.

grounding: Irawati, brilliant at analysis but struggling with organisation and social skills, learns to see strengths and gaps without shame and works on each.
